ai_risk_management.title: AI risk is risk, not magic
ai_risk_management.explanation: AI systems carry the same classes of risk as software - confidentiality, integrity, availability - plus model-specific risks like bias and hallucination.
ai_risk_management.practical: Assess AI with the same discipline you use for any critical system, then add the model-specific layers.

ai_risk_management.title: Risk cannot be eliminated
ai_risk_management.explanation: Security reduces risk to a level the organization accepts. A governance process decides what that level is.
ai_risk_management.practical: Define a risk appetite so controls and exceptions are judged consistently.

ai_risk_management.title: Risk changes over time
ai_risk_management.explanation: New threats, new users, new data, and model drift all change the risk profile. Assessment is continuous, not a one-time gate.
ai_risk_management.practical: Re-run the risk assessment whenever the system or its context changes.

threat_modeling.title: Model before you build
threat_modeling.explanation: Threat modeling names the components, the trust boundaries, and the ways an attacker can cross them before you deploy.
threat_modeling.practical: Draw the architecture, mark each boundary, and ask what could go wrong at each one.

threat_modeling.title: Threat to control to residual risk
threat_modeling.explanation: A good model flows from threat to attack vector to business impact, then to a control, then to the risk that remains.
threat_modeling.practical: Every control you add should be traceable to a specific threat it reduces.

threat_modeling.title: Frameworks structure the work
threat_modeling.explanation: STRIDE gives a high-level list of threat classes, MITRE ATT&CK names attacker behaviors, and OWASP maps known LLM weaknesses.
threat_modeling.practical: Use them as checklists to make sure you did not forget a whole class of attack.

defense_in_depth.title: Layers, not a wall
defense_in_depth.explanation: No single control is perfect. Defense in depth stacks independent controls so one failure does not end the defense.
defense_in_depth.practical: Combine gateway filtering, output validation, and human approval rather than relying on one.

defense_in_depth.title: Controls must not depend on each other
defense_in_depth.explanation: If every layer uses the same weakness, the layers collapse together. Vary the techniques across layers.
defense_in_depth.practical: Mix technical controls, process controls, and human checks.

least_privilege.title: Give the minimum access
least_privilege.explanation: Users, processes, and models should have only the access they need for their task, nothing more.
least_privilege.practical: Scope retrieval to the current user, limit who can see logs, and keep model keys separate.

least_privilege.title: It limits blast radius
least_privilege.explanation: When one account is compromised, least privilege decides how much damage the attacker can do.
least_privilege.practical: Apply it to people and to the AI system's own tool and data access.

zero_trust.title: Never trust, always verify
zero_trust.explanation: Assume a breach is possible on the network and in the pipeline. Every request is authenticated and authorized on its own.
zero_trust.practical: Do not trust a prompt because it came from an internal user or a logged-in session.

zero_trust.title: Treat prompts as untrusted input
zero_trust.explanation: A prompt can carry injection payloads no matter who sends it. Validate, filter, and verify before acting.
zero_trust.practical: Treat the model boundary like any other untrusted network boundary.

human_in_the_loop.title: A human owns the decision
human_in_the_loop.explanation: For high-impact actions the model proposes and a person disposes. The model is a decision aid, not the authority.
human_in_the_loop.practical: Require approval before the AI takes irreversible or high-stakes actions.

human_in_the_loop.title: Human review has its own cost
human_in_the_loop.explanation: Approval loops slow things down and people rubber-stamp when overloaded. Reserve them for the decisions that matter.
human_in_the_loop.practical: Use automation where consequences are low and humans where they are high.

secure_ai_lifecycle.title: Security before deployment
secure_ai_lifecycle.explanation: AI security starts at the business goal, then flows through data, model, threat assessment, controls, governance, and only then deployment.
secure_ai_lifecycle.practical: Address risk early because retrofitting controls after launch is expensive and incomplete.

secure_ai_lifecycle.title: Every phase has a job
secure_ai_lifecycle.explanation: Data quality feeds model behavior, model choice sets the attack surface, and controls decide the residual risk.
secure_ai_lifecycle.practical: Track decisions from each phase so the final recommendation is defensible.

model_monitoring.title: Watch behavior, not just uptime
model_monitoring.explanation: A model that is up and fast can still be drifting, biased, or wrong. Monitor outputs and outcomes.
model_monitoring.practical: Track accuracy against real outcomes, fairness across groups, and unexpected prompt patterns.

model_monitoring.title: Monitoring feeds governance
model_monitoring.explanation: Evidence from production justifies keeping, adjusting, or retiring a system.
model_monitoring.practical: Turn monitoring findings into periodic governance reviews.

incident_response_for_ai.title: Plan for the AI-specific incident
incident_response_for_ai.explanation: Incidents include prompt injections, data leaks through prompts, model poisoning, and harmful outputs - not just server failures.
incident_response_for_ai.practical: Extend the incident playbook with AI-specific detection and response steps.

incident_response_for_ai.title: Contain and learn
incident_response_for_ai.explanation: Isolate the model, stop the risky channel, preserve evidence, then update the risk assessment and controls.
incident_response_for_ai.practical: Log everything so an AI incident can be reconstructed and explained.

nist_ai_rmf.title: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
nist_ai_rmf.explanation: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework structures AI risk work in four functions: govern, map, measure, and manage.
nist_ai_rmf.practical: Govern sets the rules, map finds the risks, measure quantifies them, and manage applies controls.

nist_ai_rmf.title: A reference, not a checklist
nist_ai_rmf.explanation: The framework guides how to think about AI risk and adapt it to your context.
nist_ai_rmf.practical: Use its functions to structure your assessment and your report.

owasp_llm_top10.title: The LLM weakness catalog
owasp_llm_top10.explanation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications lists the common weaknesses: prompt injection, data leakage, training data poisoning, and more.
owasp_llm_top10.practical: Match each identified risk to an OWASP LLM category to communicate with a shared vocabulary.

owasp_llm_top10.title: Prompt injection leads the list
owasp_llm_top10.explanation: Injection is the defining LLM weakness because prompts are both input and instructions.
owasp_llm_top10.practical: Design gateways that treat prompt content as untrusted.

mitre_attack_concepts.title: Attacker behavior, named
mitre_attack_concepts.explanation: MITRE ATT&CK catalogs how attackers operate across reconnaissance, initial access, persistence, and more.
mitre_attack_concepts.practical: Use it to imagine how an attacker would target the AI system at each stage.

mitre_attack_concepts.title: High level here
mitre_attack_concepts.explanation: This lab uses ATT&CK concepts at a high level to keep the focus on risk reasoning, not taxonomy.
mitre_attack_concepts.practical: Name the behavior, then reason about the control that disrupts it.

stride_concepts.title: Six threat classes
stride_concepts.explanation: STRIDE stands for Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
stride_concepts.practical: Walk the architecture once per letter to catch classes you might miss.

stride_concepts.title: A conversation starter
stride_concepts.explanation: STRIDE is a high-level lens that turns 'what could go wrong' into structured categories.
stride_concepts.practical: Tag each identified risk with its STRIDE class.

iso_iec_42001.title: A management system for AI
iso_iec_42001.explanation: ISO/IEC 42001 provides a management system for AI governance, similar in spirit to ISO 27001 for information security.
iso_iec_42001.practical: It organizes policy, risk, and oversight so AI use is repeatable and auditable.

iso_iec_42001.title: Educational overview only
iso_iec_42001.explanation: This lab teaches the concepts. It does not certify or guarantee compliance with the standard.
iso_iec_42001.practical: Use it to understand how enterprises structure AI governance programs.

eu_ai_act.title: Risk-based regulation
eu_ai_act.explanation: The EU AI Act regulates AI by risk tier, with the strictest duties for high-risk uses like employment and medical decisions.
eu_ai_act.practical: Know the tier of your system because it changes the controls and documentation expected.

eu_ai_act.title: Educational overview only
eu_ai_act.explanation: This lab explains the concept of risk tiers. It does not provide legal advice or compliance certification.
eu_ai_act.practical: Use it to understand why governance documentation matters before deployment.
